outcome: No exact function, closed-form generating function, or resolution of the self-avoiding walk counting problem has been found since 26 January 2024; only incremental, traditional (non-AI) improvements to bounds and asymptotic estimates surfaced.
summary: The problem asks for an exact function (closed-form generating function or counting formula) for the number of n-step self-avoiding walks on a lattice — a classic unsolved problem in combinatorics/statistical mechanics, with no known formula except for degenerate or highly restricted cases (e.g. spiral walks on the triangular lattice, known since decades before 2024). I searched broadly for any 2024–2026 claim of an exact solution, a proof of the connective constant's value on the square (or other non-hexagonal) lattice, or any AI/ML-driven result, and found none. The Wikipedia article 'Self-avoiding walk' (checked as of its current revision) still states plainly that 'there is currently no known formula, although there are rigorous methods of approximation,' and that the exact connective constant is known only for the hexagonal lattice (Duminil-Copin & Smirnov, 2010/2012 — well before the window). Within the window I found only incremental, traditional-mathematics work: Qidong He's arXiv:2508.01993 (submitted Sept 2025) improves upper bounds on the *weighted* connective constant via dominant-eigenvalue matrix methods (no AI, no exact formula, problem remains open); and an arXiv:2504.13093 paper (April 2025) recasts SAW counting as a lattice-point-counting problem to derive *asymptotic* estimates for square-lattice SAWs across dimensions — again not an exact function and not AI-based. Neither paper changes what a careful person would write for this bullet: the exact enumeration function remains unknown. I also searched specifically for AI/ML angles (LLM-assisted conjecture generation, transformers, reinforcement learning applied to SAW counting) and found no work connecting any AI system to this specific problem; adjacent transformer-learning-random-walks papers (e.g. arXiv:2511.23239) are about learning simple random walks as a toy ML problem, unrelated to enumerating self-avoiding walks or contributing to the mathematical open problem. Given the volume and specificity of the search terms tried, and that the Wikipedia article itself shows no update to its 'no known formula' language, I am confident this is a genuine 'nothing happened, and no AI involvement' case.
competing_reading: One could argue the two 2025 bound/asymptotic papers constitute 'progress' worth a status of 'progress' rather than 'open', since a bound on the connective constant did move (He's paper) — but per §3.1, an existence/enumeration-type problem ('find a function to model n-step SAWs') is not the same as a 'largest known value' or 'value of a constant' bullet where a moved bound counts as the question itself. The bullet as phrased asks for an exact modeling function, not for the tightest bound on the connective constant (which is the separate, related open problem of determining μ exactly). Because no such function was found and the connective-constant bound movement is for a genuinely different (though closely related) question, I classified this as 'open' with no_change_found true rather than 'progress'. If the harness intends this bullet to be read as encompassing connective-constant bound improvements, 'progress' with ai_role 'none' would be the alternative classification.
what_would_settle_it: An exact closed-form counting function or generating function for n-step self-avoiding walks on a standard lattice (square, cubic, etc.) — which would itself resolve one of the most famous open problems in combinatorics — or, short of that, clearer evidence on whether the bullet is meant to include connective-constant bound movements as in-scope 'progress'.
